Empirical Research Plan: Do Employers Discriminate Against Resumes with African-American–Sounding Names?

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Randomized Controlled Trial (field-experiment / correspondence study).

Justification  
• Names that signal race are assigned to resumes by the researcher using a random mechanism.  
• Because treatment is randomized prior to any employer decision, potential outcomes are, in expectation, independent of treatment status.  
• With randomization, the naïve difference in average callback rates is an unbiased estimator of the causal effect of perceived race.  
• Regression adjustment (e.g., including city, industry, job-level fixed effects) can improve precision without affecting identification.

Why not DiD, IV, RDD, etc.?  
There is no timing shock, instrument, or running variable; treatment is assigned ex-ante by the researcher.

====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if resume i is assigned a distinctively African-American–sounding name  
T_i = 0 if assigned a distinctively White-sounding name

Control group  
Resumes with White names serve as the counterfactual.

Treatment timing / event date  
Immediate and simultaneous at the moment the resume is sent; no staggered timing is necessary for identification.

Other experimental factors  
• Resume quality Q_i ∈ {High, Low} is orthogonally randomized.  
• Two cities (Boston, Chicago) and multiple industries/occupations are covered; these are not treatments but can be used for heterogeneity analysis.

====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Successful Randomization  
The name assignment procedure is truly random and independent of all observed and unobserved resume characteristics (aside from the orthogonally randomized quality dimension).  
→ Plausible: assignment is done by the researchers with a random number generator.

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
The callback outcome for any given resume is unaffected by the name assignments on other resumes.  
→ Plausible because employers evaluate each “applicant” independently; however, if the same firm receives multiple resumes from the study, spillovers could occur (see Threats).

A3. No Differential Measurement Error in Outcome  
Callbacks are recorded identically for both racial groups (e.g., identical voicemail setup, same phone service reliability).  
→ Plausible; researchers control the voicemail and e-mail response system.

A4. Exclusion of Other Signals  
Names convey race but do not systematically convey other productivity-relevant traits that differ between treatment and control.  
→ Mostly plausible but not perfect; distinctively Black names may be correlated in employers’ minds with socioeconomic status or neighborhood of residence. This cannot be fully ruled out but is inherent in studying labor-market discrimination via names.

====================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Within-Firm Correlation / Spillovers  
If an employer receives both a “White” and a “Black” resume, learning or suspicion could bias estimates.  
Mitigation:  
• Send at most one resume per job opening (or randomize which résumés go to which ads).  
• Cluster standard errors at the job-ad (employer) level to account for residual correlation.

T2. Other Information Embedded in Names  
Names could signal socioeconomic background, gender, or neighborhood quality in addition to race.  
Mitigation:  
• Use a large, commonly-used pool of names documented to differ mainly in perceived race.  
• Acknowledge in interpretation that estimates capture employer response to all signals embedded in the name—consistent with most discrimination definitions.

T3. Detection of the Experiment (“Fake-resume bias”)  
Employers might discover that applications are fictitious and respond differently by treatment arm.  
Mitigation:  
• Design realistic, internally consistent resumes.  
• Use different résumé formats, addresses, and cover letters.  
• Drop any employer that explicitly flags a résumé as suspicious; perform robustness analyses excluding late-period observations that might be more likely to be detected.

====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # regression with fast FE and clustering
library(ggplot2)         # plots

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
df <- fread("resumes_callbacks.csv")   # one row per resume

# Expected raw columns: 
#   callback (0/1), black_name (0/1), high_quality (0/1), 
#   city (Boston/Chicago), industry, occ_type, ad_id, eoe_flag

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
df[, `:=`(
  treat_black   = black_name,          # 1 = African-American name
  quality_high  = high_quality,        # 1 = high quality resume
  city_boston   = as.integer(city=="Boston")
)]

# Interaction term, if desired
df[, black_x_quality := treat_black * quality_high]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Specification: Linear Probability Model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
main <- feols(callback ~ treat_black + quality_high + black_x_quality |
                city + industry + occ_type,   # absorb fixed effects
              data = df,
              cluster = ~ad_id)               # cluster by job ad
summary(main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check: Logistic Regression w/ Clustered SE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
robust_logit <- feglm(callback ~ treat_black + quality_high + black_x_quality +
                        city + industry + occ_type,
                      data = df, family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                      cluster = ~ad_id)
summary(robust_logit)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Randomization Inference (Optional)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Shuffle treatment 1000 times to create placebo distribution
set.seed(123)
placebo_dist <- replicate(1000, {
  df[, placebo_treat := sample(treat_black)]
  coef(feols(callback ~ placebo_treat | city + industry + occ_type,
             data = df, cluster = ~ad_id))[1]
})
observed <- coef(main)["treat_black"]
p_value <- mean(abs(placebo_dist) >= abs(observed))
print(p_value)
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Based on prior research and descriptive tabulations:  
• Direction: résumés with African-American–sounding names receive fewer callbacks.  
• Approximate magnitude: White names ≈ 10–11% callback rate; Black names ≈ 6–7% → a gap of roughly −4 percentage points (about a 40% relative decline).  
• Interaction: Higher résumé quality raises callbacks for both groups but likely does not close the gap; in fact, the Black–White differential may widen slightly for high-quality resumes.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Randomized Experiment)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Successful random assignment of names ............. 1  
C2: Baseline covariate balance verified ............... 1  
C3: SUTVA holds (no interference/spillovers) .......... 0.5  
C4: No differential measurement error in callbacks .... 1  
C5: Sufficient statistical power ...................... 1  

Total (out of 5) ...................................... 4.5  

====================================================================
End of Plan
